extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and legal practitioners
extracted.subtask_short: rehearing and equitable profits in patent suits
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing motions for rehearing in patent infringement cases (grounds of newly discovered evidence or defenses, petition formalities, notice, diligence, laches, scope of reopening) and the equitable accounting of profits (definition, scope, classification, and mode of computation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for rehearing — newly discovered evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal ground for a rehearing is the discovery of new evidence since the termination of the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No rehearing will be granted where the alleged new evidence is immaterial or cumulative, would not lead to a change in the decree, was known to the party or his counsel at the former hearing, or could then have been discovered and presented by the exercise of proper diligence. (Includes cases: Miller v. Liggett & Myers Tobacco Co., Munson v. City of New York, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Immaterial or cumulative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rehearing will be denied to admit immaterial or cumulative evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and authorities: Hoe v. Kahler; Spill v. Celluloid Mfg. Co.; Munson v. Mayor of New York. A rehearing will not be ordered to admit cumulative evidence (Pfan-Schmidt v. P. H. Kelly Mercantile Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: New evidence must be capable of changing the result
rubrics_metrics.description: No rehearing will be granted unless the new evidence would change the result of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Starling v. St. Paul Plow Works; United States v. Gunning. A rehearing will be afforded only when new facts would have influenced the court's decree or tend to settle an issue (e.g., jurisdictional facts, later-issued patents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing not allowed if evidence known or obtainable with diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rehearing is barred where the new evidence was known to the party or his counsel at the time of the former trial or could have been discovered by proper diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Colgate v. Western Union Telegraph Co.; Ready Roofing Co. v. Taylor; Hicks v. Ferdinand. The knowledge and diligence of counsel are regarded as those of the party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of defective documentary evidence (drawings)
rubrics_metrics.description: A question of fact will not be re-heard merely because drawings first offered were defective unless the new evidence is so clear and positive that an entirely different case is presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: Hayes v. Dayton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and formalities for motion for rehearing (new evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion for rehearing must be signed by counsel, sworn to by the party, clearly allege the new evidence and its discovery, and state in detail the efforts made at the former hearing to ascertain and produce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due notice must be given to the opposite party and an opportunity to answer. The petition must show due diligence and why the evidence was not produced before; if satisfied, court may allow supplemental bill and take additional testimony which together with prior evidence is presented to the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental bill practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice is to petition for leave to file a supplemental bill setting up newly discovered evidence and for rehearing when the supplemental bill is ready.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will examine counter affidavits; if evidence is cumulative or application unreasonably delayed, motion denied (Blandy v. Griffith). If allowed, the supplemental bill and additional testimony and counterproof are taken and the whole record considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing where foreign or intervening patent affects jurisdiction or priority
rubrics_metrics.description: A case may be opened for further evidence and rehearing when a foreign patent supposed prior is found to be subsequent, or where a judgment in another court between same parties on same issues is rendered since trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Spring v. Domestic Sewing Mach. Co.; instances where new facts settle jurisdictional disputes or priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: No rehearing based on less persuasive prior-use evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: No rehearing will be granted on ground of newly discovered evidence of prior use when that evidence is less persuasive than the evidence on the former trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: American Bell Telephone Co. v. People's Telephone Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing on ground of surprise — duty to seek continuance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party was surprised by opponent's testimony but did not ask for a continuance to investigate and answer, later discovery that the testimony could have been contradicted does not warrant reopening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But if new facts have occurred since trial or material facts then existing were unknown and since discovered, rehearing may be allowed. Cases: Barker v. Stowe; Hitchcock v. Tremaine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for rehearing — newly discovered defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A rehearing may be granted for the existence of a defense not set up in the answer and not previously presented to the court, where the defense came to defendant's knowledge since the former hearing or was withheld for approved reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court is guided by the same principles applied to newly discovered evidence. Affidavits supporting such petition must state each new defense and account for previous failure to present it. If defense could not change the ultimate result or was withheld for improper reasons, rehearing may be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit specificity and positive proof requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit supporting a motion for rehearing is insufficient if it merely states general efforts; it must state what efforts were made and provide positive proof that the new evidence or defense could not have been obtained earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Page v. Holmes Burglar Alarm Telegraph Co.; Barker v. Stowe; De Florez v. Raynolds (ignorance or incapacity of counsel is no ground).

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition signing and swearing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition to re-open must be signed by counsel, sworn to before a disinterested magistrate, and must be clear in allegations, fully disclose the new evidence and its discovery, and set forth the diligence used before the former hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Allis v. Stowell; Spill v. Celluloid Mfg. Co.; Reeves v. Keystone Bridge Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and adversary opportunity — not ex parte
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for rehearing after a decree is not ex parte; it requires notice to the opposite party and a chance to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Giant Powder Co. v. California Vigorit Powder Co.; Blandy v. Griffith (delay consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches and undue delay as grounds for denial
rubrics_metrics.description: Laches in applying for rehearing or unreasonable delay in moving to reopen (e.g., long delay after discovery or after paying execution) will form grounds for denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hoe v. Kahler (laches); Blandy v. Griffith (delay of a year and a half too long); Doubleday v. Sherman (eleven months after paying execution too late).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing will not be used to reprepare the case
rubrics_metrics.description: A rehearing will not be granted merely so the defendant can prepare the case anew, to remedy counsel neglect, or solely because counsel were surprised by unexpected claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Coburn v. Schroeder; Day v. Schwab; Everest v. Buffalo Lubricating Oil Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope on rehearing — old and new evidence considered together
rubrics_metrics.description: When a rehearing is granted and new evidence admitted, the old and new evidence are opened and considered together by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Reed v. Lawrence; Henry v. Francestown Soapstone Co.; Reeves v. Keystone Bridge Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing on misquotation or minor errors
rubrics_metrics.description: A rehearing will not be granted on the ground that the court misquoted testimony if the misquotation did not affect the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: Torrent v. Duluth Lumber Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing where issues are narrowed by disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer narrowing a claim does not change the issues such that a rehearing is required; it narrows but does not broaden the prior issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Coburn v. Schroeder; disclaimer of part of a claim limits scope rather than expanding it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing for additional argument (no new facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rehearing may be made on the ground of necessity for further argument and consideration even where no new facts are presented and the issues are unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. Chrolithion Collar & Cuff Co.; also may be allowed to review recent Supreme Court decisions, with testimony preserved for future use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable profits distinct from legal damages
rubrics_metrics.description: "Profits" in equity and "damages" at law are distinct in theory and mode of computation; each should be examined and expressed independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Goodyear Dental Vulcanite Co. v. Van Antwerp; discussion that profits in equity include all benefits derived by defendant without reference to amount plaintiff might otherwise have received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity's power to compel accounting for unlawful gains
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of equity has power to order a defendant to account for unlawful gains from infringement where it has jurisdiction over him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power historically exercised in chancery and adopted by U.S. courts; act of 1870 sanctioned recovery of profits and damages in equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of profits in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits in equity include all pecuniary benefits which the defendant has derived from the infringement and are regarded in equity as the property of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ascertain amount, defendant ordered to render account and final decree directs payment of sum ascertained; account taken before a master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of taking account — master and binding rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The master takes the account, investigates and reports net amount, and is bound by certain rules concerning items with which defendant must be charged or credited and the evidence required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules differ by class of infringement (use/making & use vs manufacture & sale) and govern admissible items and credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of infringement cases for accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principal classes for computing profits: (1) unlawful use, or making and use of the patented invention; (2) unlawful sale, or manufacture and sale of the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items on each side of the account differ substantially between the two classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits must be due to the patented invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits are not to be accounted for unless they are due to the invention covered by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Brady v. Atlantic Works; Kennedy v. Hazelton (no profit decreed for use of a void patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of profits where defendant used the plaintiff's device
rubrics_metrics.description: Where defendant has used plaintiff's device, it is presumed there might have been some profits and an account of them will be ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case references: Sargent v. Yale Lock Mfg. Co.; Calhoun v. Bertrand; Bardett v. Estey; Elizabeth v. Pavement Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory decrees — gains, savings and advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory decree directing an account of 'gains, savings, and advantages' in addition to profits, and awarding costs, is proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Coburn v. Schroeder; such interlocutory orders are commonly used to secure the accounting process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's choice of general or special profits
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff may recover the profits due to use of his improvement on a bill praying for either general or special profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Graham v. Mason; plaintiff's pleadings may seek general or special relief with respect to profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: No account for benefits not received
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no benefits are received by the defendant from the infringement, there are no profits to be accounted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities cited in text: instances where accounting is inappropriate absent realized benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustee analogy — limits and caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity sometimes treats an infringer as a trustee for purposes of accounting, but the defendant is not truly a trustee; the analogy helps explain remedies but must not be taken to obliterate doctrinal distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion includes limits on trustee analogy; see Tilghman v. Proctor and related sections for relation of infringer to patentee.
